semanticBlocks: 1. Why C4

The C4 model gives architects a shared zoom lens. Instead of one overloaded drawing trying to satisfy executives, developers, security reviewers, and operators at once, C4 splits the conversation into Context, Container, Component, and Code. Each level answers a different question without forcing readers to decode implementation detail before they understand the system boundary.

The SPA currently demonstrates the first two zoom levels. The System Context view shows platform actors and neighboring systems. Clicking a system drills into its containers: Eventhouse, Lakehouse layers, Bicep modules, Deployment Stacks, Key Vault, Azure Functions, Copilot agents, and KQL dashboards. That mirrors the reference architecture style used for Fabric, the monitoring platform, the certificate automation, and the security platform.
C4 vs Traditional UML
2. Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) as Markdown

Architecture diagrams show shape. ADRs show intent. The Studio pairs the C4 browser with decision records so a viewer can ask why a pattern exists, who benefits, what trade-offs were accepted, and what would justify changing the decision later.

The reference ADR style is intentionally lightweight: title, status, context, decision, and consequences. Markdown keeps the format readable in Git, reviewable in pull requests, and publishable to Confluence without converting the source of truth into a screenshot or slide deck.
Sample ADR Header

# ADR-008 — One Shared Eventstream per Fabric Workspace Status: Accepted Date: 2026-05-29 ## Context A Fabric workspace can receive events from multiple Event Hub sources. Creating one Eventstream per source multiplies idle capacity burn before real throughput becomes the limiting factor. ## Decision Use exactly one shared Eventstream per workspace, named es_{workspace}_{env}. Add new sources to that stream and route by eventType, source, or another explicit payload field. ## Consequences - Lower idle Capacity Unit baseline - Simpler routing and fewer objects to operate - KQL update policies handle downstream classification - A second Eventstream requires a documented exception
3. Diagrams as Code (PlantUML + Mermaid)

The Build 2026 refresh keeps diagram source text front and center. PlantUML is best for C4-style system structure, component boundaries, and sequence flows. Mermaid is excellent for simple flowcharts, dependency chains, and documentation embedded directly in Markdown. Both formats let engineers review architecture changes with the same workflow used for application code.

This matters because the source documents use PlantUML-backed architecture diagrams for Fabric, the notification pipeline, the monitoring platform, and certificate automation. A diagram change can travel with a Bicep module, notebook, KQL function, or ADR change instead of arriving later as a stale export.
PlantUML Context Snippet

@startuml !include <C4/C4_Context> title Fabric Real-Time Architecture — Sanitized Example Person(engineer, "Platform Engineer", "Reviews capacity, routing, and incident paths") System_Boundary(workspace, "Fabric Workspace") { System(eventstream, "Shared Eventstream", "Fans in Event Hub sources") System(eventhouse, "Eventhouse", "Hot KQL analytics and update policies") System(lakehouse, "Lakehouse", "Delta tables for historical analytics") } System_Ext(eventhub, "Event Hub Namespace", "Generic event ingress") Rel(engineer, eventhouse, "Queries alerts and trends") Rel(eventhub, eventstream, "Sends events") Rel(eventstream, eventhouse, "Routes raw events") Rel(eventstream, lakehouse, "Persists cold path") @enduml
Mermaid Flow Snippet

flowchart LR Decide[Decide in ADR] --> Diagram[Update PlantUML or Mermaid] Diagram --> Review[Pull request review] Review --> Publish[Confluence API publish] Publish --> Maintain[Keep architecture living]
4. The Eventstream Topology Decision

The clearest ADR walkthrough in the reference set is the Eventstream topology decision. The design question was whether a Fabric workspace should create one Eventstream per Event Hub source or one shared Eventstream that fans in multiple sources. The accepted answer: one shared Eventstream per workspace.

The reason is operational and economic. Each active Eventstream has an idle Capacity Unit floor. On a constrained capacity, many nearly idle streams can consume a meaningful share of the SKU before actual event volume arrives. Because Fabric Eventstream can accept multiple Event Hub sources and route into multiple KQL tables or destinations, the additional streams mostly add baseline burn and operational surface area.
Sanitized Topology

Event Hub namespace ├─ source-a-events ├─ source-b-events └─ source-c-events ↓ Fabric Eventstream: es_platform_dev ↓ route by source / eventType Eventhouse raw tables ↓ KQL update policies Classified alert actions + lakehouse history
5. Confluence Publishing (Markdown → Confluence via API)

The reference workflow treats Markdown as the authoring source and Confluence as the publishing surface. Architecture pages carry metadata, diagrams, tables, and code snippets in Git. A publishing script renders the Markdown, preserves PlantUML or Mermaid blocks, and updates Confluence through the API so the public-facing collaboration page reflects reviewed source.

This pattern gives engineers the benefits of code review while still meeting stakeholders where they already read documentation. Product owners, operations teams, and auditors see the polished Confluence page. Engineers maintain the Markdown, diagram source, and ADRs beside the implementation.
Publishing Shape

Markdown article ├─ front matter: version, tags, status ├─ C4 / PlantUML diagrams ├─ ADR sections ├─ implementation tables └─ footer references ↓ sanitize and render Confluence API update ↓ Reviewed architecture page with stable links
6. The Living Architecture Pattern

The living architecture pattern is the core lesson across the Fabric, monitoring, notification, and certificate automation references. Architecture stays current when the diagram, decision, and implementation travel together. A Fabric notebook structure change updates the C4 container diagram. A topology change creates or amends an ADR. A pipeline change updates the publishing source and Confluence page in the same review cycle.

The SPA makes that pattern tangible. ClojureScript data renders the interactive C4 model. Markdown ADRs explain accepted trade-offs. PlantUML and Mermaid examples show how static diagrams can remain diffable. The result is not just a portfolio demo; it is a model for keeping platform architecture understandable after the original launch meeting ends.
1. From Chat to Agentic

The important shift is not better prompt engineering. The shift is moving from chat as a text box to chat as a control plane. A useful agent reads the user's intent, chooses the correct capability, gathers evidence, calls a tool, and returns a verifiable result. The prompt matters, but the tool contract matters more.

The reference pattern is intentionally boring: HTTP triggers, scheduled jobs, Python or PowerShell scripts, API calls, and structured responses. A model adds judgment at the language layer: triage, summarization, prioritization, and routing. Deterministic code still owns identity, authorization, state changes, retries, and audit logging.

That split is the 90/10 rule in practice. Ninety percent of the workflow is reliable automation. Ten percent is model-assisted judgment that helps decide which deterministic path to take next. The agent should not become the business process; it should make the business process easier to operate.
From Search Box to Workbench
2. The Model Context Protocol (MCP)

MCP gives agents a standard way to discover tools, understand schemas, and invoke operations without every client inventing a custom adapter. It does not replace APIs. It packages APIs, CLIs, documentation, and local context into a predictable tool surface that agent clients can reason over.

That is why MCP fits the SPA's original thesis: agents should use the interfaces developers already trust. Azure CLI, GitHub CLI, Fabric REST APIs, Graph API, and documentation search remain the underlying source of truth. MCP makes those capabilities discoverable and composable for the model.

The practical design rule is simple: expose the smallest useful tool surface. A read-only inventory tool can run autonomously. A role assignment, deletion, status transition, or outbound message must stop at a confirmation boundary with a plain-language summary of what will change.
3. Skills as Reusable Capabilities

Skills are the reusable unit above tools. A tool says, "I can call this endpoint." A skill says, "Here is the job, the decision policy, the evidence to gather, the voice to use, and the safe stopping points." The platform team uses skills for dispatching work, investigating tickets, logging time, reviewing PRs, deploying Fabric pipelines, updating documentation, and closing the day.

The most important skill rule is one job per skill. A dispatcher should dispatch. A worklog skill should log work. An investigator should gather context and propose a plan only after evidence supports it. Small skills can chain together, but each one remains understandable, testable, and replaceable.
Sample Skill Structure

# SKILL.md --- name: ticket-investigator description: Start a structured investigation on a work item. allowed-tools: - bash - grep - view - scripts/context_bundle.py - scripts/set_flow.py --- ## Purpose Gather evidence before proposing a plan. ## Inputs - Work item key, sanitized as INFRA-### in public examples - Current markdown case file - Operator goal or blocking question ## Workflow 1. Load the context bundle. 2. Ask only clarifying questions needed to reach confidence. 3. Gather evidence with read-only tools first. 4. Propose a plan with risks, commands, and rollback notes. 5. Stop for operator approval before destructive actions. ## Safety - Never expose secrets or tokens. - Never close or delete without explicit confirmation. - Record decisions in markdown so the diff is reviewable.

That structure turns a general-purpose model into an operational teammate. The skill constrains the work, the tool surface provides capabilities, and the markdown file holds the durable state. When the operator says "next ticket," the router can choose a dispatcher skill; when a ticket is active, an investigator skill can gather evidence; when work is done, a worklog skill can update the source-of-truth file.
4. Tool-Calling, Verified

Tool-calling agents are powerful because they can do more than write prose. They can query systems, run tests, fetch documentation, open pull requests, update markdown, or call a workflow. They are also risky for the same reason. Verification is the boundary that makes the pattern usable.

The platform team's safe default is read, summarize, and propose. Read-only tools can run with high autonomy. Write tools require the agent to show the intended change, the target system, the reason, and the verification step. The operator approves the action or asks for a narrower plan.

This is also the answer to prompt injection. Untrusted text may influence what the model says, but it must not silently decide what the system does. External input is treated like user input in any secure application: validate it, scope it, and keep privileged effects behind deterministic checks.
5. The Operator-in-the-Loop Model

The operator loop is event-driven rather than fully sequential. Safe background agents can investigate, summarize, and prepare changes while the human focuses on the highest-priority station. When an agent reaches a decision point, it pops up with evidence and choices. The operator can accept, reject, narrow scope, or take over interactively.

Autopilot is appropriate for safe operations: indexing documentation, reading logs, grouping stale tickets, drafting follow-ups, or running tests. Irreversible work stays human-gated: access grants, production deployments, deletion, ticket closure, external messages, or anything that changes customer-visible state.
Autonomy Bands
6. Why Markdown-Driven State Wins for Agents

Agents need durable state they can read, diff, cite, and update without hiding decisions inside a chat transcript. Markdown files are a surprisingly strong substrate: they are human-readable, git-tracked, mergeable, searchable, and easy for tools to parse. A work item becomes a file with description, investigation, actions, follow-up, and flow labels.

That gives the operator three advantages. First, the current state is visible without opening a proprietary UI. Second, every change has a git diff and commit history. Third, CI/CD can reconcile the file to downstream systems through APIs, making the markdown file the source of truth rather than a stale note.
File-Driven Agent State

issues/INFRA-###.md ├── Description # What the work is and why it matters ├── Investigation # Evidence, commands, findings, links ├── Actions # Reverse-chronological WORKLOG and COMMENT entries └── Follow-up # Current status and concrete next steps flow:queue → flow:active → flow:waiting → flow:done commit + push → GitHub Actions → API sync → verified downstream state

The same pattern works for service requests, approvals, backlog items, and operational runbooks. The agent can plan against the file, update the file, and prove what changed. The human can review the diff. The pipeline can push only the approved state to the target system. That is the operator loop in durable form.
Why It Beats Hidden State
1. Effects: Audit vs Modify vs Deny vs DeployIfNotExists

Azure Policy effect choice is the architecture decision behind every governance rule. The SPA intentionally exposes effect next to scope and compliance because an enterprise policy program cannot be judged by assignment count alone. A safe rollout usually starts with audit, graduates routine metadata to modify, reserves deny for high-confidence guardrails, and uses DeployIfNotExists when missing platform plumbing must be deployed after evaluation.

This effect model mirrors the operating runbook mindset: identify the failing control, check identity and scope, remediate the resource or assignment, then document the outcome. Policy is not a static catalog. It is a closed-loop system that needs owners, evidence, escalation paths, and a clear line between non-blocking hygiene and hard safety boundaries.
Assignment Categories Shown in the Dashboard
2. The Tagging Governance Pattern (modify-effect, non-blocking)

The most important design choice in the refreshed article is the modify-first tagging pattern. Required tags are governance inputs: they connect resources to owners, budget centers, environments, projects, and incident routing. Blocking every deployment that misses a tag creates friction; modifying safe metadata in-flight makes the paved road easier to use while still improving reporting quality.

The dashboard treats tag governance as a platform service. A policy assignment can inherit a default from the resource group, normalize casing, or add a placeholder value that routes back to a remediation queue. That keeps delivery moving, but it also makes drift visible. The owner still needs to clean up inaccurate values; policy simply prevents missing metadata from becoming invisible technical debt.

// Modify-effect policy rule sketch for required ownership metadata { "if": { "allOf": [ { "field": "type", "notEquals": "Microsoft.Resources/subscriptions/resourceGroups" }, { "field": "tags['CostCenter']", "exists": false } ] }, "then": { "effect": "modify", "details": { "roleDefinitionIds": [ "/providers/Microsoft.Authorization/roleDefinitions/<tag-contributor-role-id>" ], "operations": [ { "operation": "add", "field": "tags['CostCenter']", "value": "[resourceGroup().tags['CostCenter']]" } ] } } }
3. Policy as Code (Bicep policy definitions, deployment via stacks)

At scale, a policy definition should not be a portal-only artifact. The article positions policy as code: definitions, initiatives, assignments, parameters, and managed identities are reviewed, deployed, and versioned through infrastructure stacks. That gives policy changes the same discipline as any other production control: pull request review, environment parameters, repeatable deployment, and rollback history.

Bicep is a natural fit for the definition and assignment layer. A stack can publish a custom policy definition, assign it at a management group or subscription scope, grant the assignment identity only the permissions needed for remediation, and expose environment-specific parameters without embedding tenant-specific IDs in the source. That makes the dashboard's numbers reproducible without leaking implementation details.
Policy-as-Code Deployment Shape

targetScope = 'managementGroup' param assignmentScope string = '/providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/<mg-name>' param requiredTags array = [ 'CostCenter', 'Environment', 'Owner', 'Project' ] resource tagPolicy 'Microsoft.Authorization/policyDefinitions@2023-04-01' = { name: 'modify-required-tags' properties: { policyType: 'Custom' mode: 'Indexed' displayName: 'Modify required resource tags' metadata: { category: 'Tag Governance' } parameters: { requiredTags: { type: 'Array' } } policyRule: loadJsonContent('policyRules/modify-required-tags.json') } } resource assignment 'Microsoft.Authorization/policyAssignments@2024-04-01' = { name: 'tag-governance-modify' scope: managementGroup('<mg-name>') identity: { type: 'SystemAssigned' } properties: { displayName: 'Tag governance — modify required tags' policyDefinitionId: tagPolicy.id parameters: { requiredTags: { value: requiredTags } } enforcementMode: 'Default' } }

Deployment stacks add lifecycle clarity. They make it easier to understand which environment owns the current assignment, whether a change is idempotent, and how to remove a deprecated assignment without leaving orphaned definitions or unmanaged role grants behind.
4. Exemptions: When and Why (request, approve, time-box)

Exemptions are not exceptions to governance; they are governed records that explain why a resource or scope is temporarily outside the standard. A healthy exemption flow starts with a request, captures business justification, assigns an approver role, records an expiration date, and keeps the remediation owner visible. The article uses role labels instead of named owners so the public version demonstrates the pattern without exposing internal accountability data.

Use exemptions when a control is correct but immediate enforcement would create unacceptable business risk: legacy migration windows, vendor constraints, emergency incident response, or platform dependencies that are being remediated in phases. Avoid permanent exemptions. If an exemption never expires, the policy is either too broad, the exception is actually a standard, or the owning team needs a migration plan.
5. Remediation Tasks (back-filling non-compliant resources)

Modify and DeployIfNotExists policies only change new or updated resources automatically. Existing resources need remediation tasks to back-fill the estate. That is why the SPA's compliance score should be read as an operations queue: identify the non-compliant set, verify the assignment identity has the required role, run remediation in a controlled scope, and monitor completion before escalating residual failures.

The runbook pattern applies here too. Start with the failing control, check permissions, confirm the target scope, execute the repair, then document what changed. If a remediation task fails, common causes include missing managed identity permissions, resources locked by deployment policy, unsupported resource types, or stale exemptions that need review.
Remediation Control Loop

Evaluate → query compliance state by assignment and scope Authorize → verify assignment identity has the minimum remediation role Remediate → create remediation task for the targeted policy assignment Monitor → track succeeded, failed, and skipped resources Document → record outcome, residual risk, and next review date

For public examples, use generic assignment names such as tag-governance-modify, placeholder scopes such as /subscriptions/<subscription-id>, and role labels instead of named exemption owners. Microsoft Learn URLs can remain exact because they are public documentation references.
6. JIT Access via PIM (eligible vs active assignments, time-bound elevation)

Policy operations sometimes require elevated access: creating a remediation task, changing an assignment, or approving a short-lived exemption. The refreshed article connects those tasks to just-in-time access through Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management. Eligible assignment means a user or group can request access; active assignment means the access is currently usable and will expire automatically after the approved duration.

The public pattern is intentionally generic. A production operations group is eligible for the minimum role needed, activates through My Access or the Azure PIM portal, enters a ticket-backed justification, waits for propagation, completes the operation, and lets access expire. The same pattern works for emergency changes and planned maintenance: no standing human access, time-bound elevation, and a written trail of why the access was used.
Why Naming Conventions Matter

Cloud sprawl starts as a readability problem. If a resource name does not reveal type, workload, environment, and region, every incident, cleanup, and cost review begins with a manual lookup. CAF-aligned naming converts the name itself into operational metadata.

The matcher game reinforces that pattern by asking players to connect resource types to compliant names. In production, the same matching happens in pull requests, deployment pipelines, inventory exports, and chargeback reviews.

Consistent naming improves ownership, cost attribution, and governance. A resource named func-coredata-prd-usw2-001 immediately reads as an example project code for a production Function App in West US 2. A name like app-final-v2 does not.
The CAF Pattern Explained
The Azure resource convention used by the demo follows a hyphenated Cloud Adoption Framework pattern:
{type}-{project}-{env}-{region}-{instance} func-project-dev-usw2-001 kv-coremon-prd-usw2-001 # coremon is an example project code umi-coredata-dev-usw2-ctl # ctl marks a control-plane identity
Resource-Type Abbreviations

The canonical table keeps names predictable across subscriptions. It is grounded in the Microsoft CAF abbreviation guidance and extended with common deployment, identity, data, analytics, network, monitoring, and Fabric-adjacent resource types used by modern Azure platforms.
Special Cases
Not every Azure service can use the hyphenated pattern exactly. CAF is a convention, but Azure resource-name rules still win.
Fabric Artifact Naming

Microsoft Fabric artifacts use a different but complementary convention. Instead of hyphenated Azure resource names, Fabric workspace items use underscore-delimited prefixes that make the artifact type, domain, and medallion layer visible in the workspace list. Common wildcard patterns include lh_*_brz, lh_*_slv, lh_*_gld, and nb_*_dq_*.
Bronze: lh_sales_brz, pl_ing_erp_sales_brz, nb_dq_sales_brz Silver: lh_sales_slv, pl_tfm_sales_brz_slv, nb_dq_sales_slv Gold: lh_sales_gld, dw_sales_gld, sm_sales_performance, rpt_sales_dashboard
Enforcement at the PR Gate

Naming conventions work when they are checked before resources exist. The PR gate should validate IaC names with the Azure Naming Tool, run the Bicep linter, and fail the build when a resource cannot be traced to the expected pattern.
Pull request opens → bicep build / bicep linter → naming-rule validation → storage and key-vault special-case checks → policy-as-code and deployment preview → merge only when names are compliant
This is the operational lesson behind the SPA. The game rewards correct matches immediately; the platform should do the same by catching drift in code review rather than after deployment.
1. Why Clojure

Rich Hickey's distinction between simple and easy matters here. Clojure is not always the easiest language in the moment, but it is unusually good at making systems simple: data is explicit, mutation is controlled, values are composable, and complexity is harder to hide behind classes and framework ceremony.

That philosophy shows up even in this tiny REPL. Examples focus on map/filter, persistent vectors, threading macros, destructuring, recursion, and atoms. In other words, the demo teaches the language through ideas that scale beyond syntax.
2. SCI — Small Clojure Interpreter

SCI is the technical trick that makes the page possible. Instead of sending code to a server-side runtime, the browser hosts an interpreter configured with an allowed namespace surface. The source initializes an SCI context once and reuses it for each evaluation, which keeps the interaction immediate while avoiding the complexity of standing up a remote REPL service.

(def sci-ctx (sci/init {:namespaces {'user {'println println}}})) (defn evaluate [code] (try {:ok true :value (pr-str (sci/eval-string* sci-ctx code))} (catch :default e {:ok false :value (str 'Error: ' (.-message e))})))
That restricted model is part of why the demo feels safe and portable. It is not pretending to be a full development environment; it is a focused in-browser evaluator with a clear trust boundary.
3. This Website Runs Clojure

The page is also a quiet statement about the broader stack: Clojure is not confined to toy REPLs or back-office batch jobs. The ecosystem comfortably spans browser code, build tooling, serverless functions, and cloud workflows. In that sense the playground is less a gimmick than a visible endpoint of a larger Clojure-first approach.
That is why the portfolio framing matters. A live REPL on a personal site says something stronger than a static code screenshot: the language is part of the operating model, not just a side hobby.
4. ClojureScript for the Browser

The surrounding site uses shadow-cljs with multiple independent browser builds, one per SPA. That is a nice fit for portfolio architecture because each demo has a separate entry point and compiled artifact, while still sharing utility namespaces. The REPL itself is just one build among many, not a special snowflake.

Interaction is delightfully direct: buttons inject sample programs into the textarea, the Evaluate button runs the current buffer, Clear resets editor and history, and Ctrl+Enter or Cmd+Enter triggers evaluation from the keyboard. Those are small touches, but they make the page feel like a real tool instead of a static showcase.
5. The Clojure Community

The final section is about culture. Clojure's community has long valued careful reasoning, durable abstractions, and generosity in teaching. Libraries like SCI are a perfect example: they enable creative experiences without abandoning the language's core values around data and explicitness.
This playground feels like a love letter because it is one. It turns a browser tab into a tiny space for exploration, which is exactly what a good REPL has always been.
Game Design

The level is intentionally small and legible: a 480×320 canvas, six static platforms, and one player rectangle with explicit velocity, grounded state, and collectible progress. The design goal is not procedural complexity; it is teaching motion through infrastructure. Each jump is a tiny routing exercise across the cloud topology.

Movement is deterministic and frame-rate aware. The update loop applies input, then gravity, then motion, then platform collision resolution. Gravity is expressed in pixels per second squared, horizontal velocity snaps to fixed left/right values, and jump impulse only fires while the player is grounded. That keeps the rules arcade-simple while still feeling responsive on desktop and mobile.
(-> state (update :player #(-> % (apply-input touch-state) (apply-gravity dt) (move-player dt) (collide-platforms (:platforms state)) clamp-bounds)) collect-items)
Azure Resource Icons

The collectibles are emoji-backed resource markers rather than sprite sheets: ⚡, ☁, 🔒, ⚙, and ★. That is a clever tradeoff for a portfolio game. It avoids asset loading, keeps the build self-contained, and still communicates compute, cloud, security, operations, and completion semantics instantly.

Collection is done with the same axis-aligned bounding box test used for platforms. When player and item rectangles overlap, the item is marked :collected true and score increments by 100. The win condition is simply every? :collected, which makes the game state machine very easy to reason about.
ClojureScript Game Engine

The strongest architectural choice is reuse. This page sits on top of a shared engine namespace that creates canvases, keeps a keys-down atom, exposes aabb? for collision detection, and provides a generic game-loop wrapper over requestAnimationFrame. The game code stays focused on platforming rules instead of browser plumbing.

That separation also makes the SPA portfolio coherent. Platformer, Invaders, Matcher, and Breakout all inherit the same rendering and timing model, so each article can talk about different mechanics without hiding the common implementation discipline underneath.
Canvas & Input System

Keyboard support uses browser keydown/keyup listeners and a set-backed atom. Touch support is implemented as a virtual d-pad appended beside the canvas. Each button updates a touch-state atom on touchstart and touchend, letting the game treat touch and keyboard as equivalent input channels.

That detail matters: it means the platformer is not just visually responsive at the 768px breakpoint; the interaction model is mobile-aware too. Combined with canvas bounds clamping and a lightweight HUD, the game remains readable even when embedded in a portfolio page rather than a dedicated fullscreen shell.
The Rounds Model: 6 Lanes, WIP=1 Each

The core operating model is a six-lane kanban board. Three lanes represent Jira infrastructure work: urgent, manual, and background. Three lanes mirror the ServiceDesk Plus support world: urgent, approval, and background. Each lane allows exactly one active ticket. When a ticket moves to waiting or done, a dispatcher pulls the next highest-scored item for that lane.

This is less about displaying cards and more about enforcing single-piece flow. The operator can see all work in flight without becoming the scheduler, because the console makes the constraint visible: only one urgent Jira item, one manual Jira item, one background Jira item, one urgent support case, one approval case, and one background support case are active at once.

Waiting work does not count against WIP. That distinction matters in operations because many tickets are blocked on an approver, vendor, user confirmation, or a system window. Moving blocked items to waiting frees the lane without losing context, while keeping the follow-up obligation explicit.
Investigation-First Skill Design (knowledge-clerk → ticket-investigator pattern)

The most important design choice is that skills do not jump straight from ticket title to remediation. A knowledge clerk checks precedent first: runbooks, prior ticket patterns, architecture notes, and known caveats. Then a ticket investigator gathers evidence, asks clarifying questions when confidence is low, and only proposes a plan when the evidence supports one.

That pattern protects operators from the classic failure mode of automation: fast, confident action against the wrong problem. The investigator skill treats a ticket as an evidence bundle, not a prompt. It can read the issue file, fetch current tracker state, inspect related cases, run command-line checks, and capture what it found before any change is made.

The result is a practical version of agentic automation: deterministic scripts perform known actions, while AI helps with triage, summarization, prioritization, and choosing the next investigative step. This follows the 90/10 rule: keep the workflow deterministic, then add intelligence where language and judgment are useful.
The Voice Wall: Internal vs End-User

Operations work has two audiences. The first is the internal operator who needs a precise investigative record: what was checked, what changed, what evidence proved it, and what remains unknown. The second is the requester or stakeholder who needs plain-language status: what happened, what they should expect, and how they can verify it.

The Voice Wall makes that split visible. WORKLOG entries are always internal voice. COMMENT entries change voice by system: Jira comments remain internal investigative voice, while SDP comments become end-user voice. That prevents the same sentence from trying to serve two incompatible purposes.

That discipline matters for auditability. A Jira ticket can preserve the operator's reasoning without sounding strange to a support requester. An SDP case can give a user clear next steps without leaking the messy internal path that led there.
Skill Composition Patterns

The demo treats Copilot skills as composable units rather than one giant assistant. One skill starts the day, another runs rounds, another investigates tickets, another writes worklogs, and another closes the day with a standup summary. Each skill owns a narrow responsibility and hands state to the next skill through markdown files and tracker APIs.
A common workday path looks like this:
start-my-day → rounds → knowledge-clerk → ticket-investigator → jira-worklog or sdp-worklog → waiting-ticket-followup → end-my-day

That sequence is intentionally boring. It mirrors how reliable operations teams already work: pick the right item, understand it, act, document, synchronize, and report. AI improves the speed and coverage of the loop, but the loop itself remains inspectable.
Markdown as the Source of Truth (push to main → CI reconciles)

The console's state model is deliberately simple: files in issues/ and cases/ are the durable operational record. Jira and ServiceDesk Plus remain the systems of engagement, but the work narrative is authored locally in markdown, committed, and reconciled by GitHub Actions on push to main.

This gives the operator a normal software-delivery workflow for operations: diffs, commits, history, reviewable text, and repeatable reconciliation. The sync jobs parse WORKLOG, COMMENT, task, link, approval, and flow markers, then call the appropriate APIs. Duplicate prevention can be handled with content hashes so a rerun does not repost the same entry.
Sample Issue File

--- key: INFRA-### summary: Capacity throttling on shared workload status: In Progress labels: [flow:active, lane:urgent, agentic:3] --- ## Description A shared platform workload is approaching throttling limits during peak processing. ## Investigation - Reviewed current capacity settings. - Compared queue depth against the last successful run. - Verified no recent firewall or identity changes explain the symptom. ## Actions ### 2026-05-20 WORKLOG: 45m — Investigated capacity throttling and validated the bottleneck was throughput, not network access. COMMENT: Confirmed capacity pressure during the peak processing window. Next step is to raise the throughput setting and monitor lag after the next run. ## Follow-up **Status:** Waiting — approval required from Approver before capacity change. - [ ] Approver confirms temporary scale-up window - [ ] Platform Engineer applies setting change - [ ] Validate queue depth after next run

The same pattern extends to support cases. A case file can carry tasks, web links, linked requests, and approval state. The file does not replace the service desk; it gives the operator an auditable way to prepare and reconcile updates without clicking through forms for every small change.

Treating markdown as operational state also makes automation reviewable. A proposed update is just a diff before it becomes an API call. That is the bridge between conversational assistance and production-grade change control.
Why This Matters at Build 2026 (the operator-as-orchestrator model)

Microsoft Build 2026 is likely to continue the shift from AI as a sidecar chat window to AI as an orchestration layer over real systems. The Copilot-Ops Console demonstrates that shift in a practical, operations-friendly form. The operator is not replaced; the operator becomes the conductor of constrained agents, deterministic scripts, and synchronized systems of record.

The model fits modern Microsoft platform patterns. Microsoft Foundry can host models and agents. Semantic Kernel can orchestrate tools. Microsoft Graph can supply identity-aware context. GitHub Actions can reconcile repository state to APIs. The key architectural decision is not which model answers the question; it is where truth, permission, approval, and audit live.

For operational teams, that means the next generation of Copilot experiences should look less like an all-knowing chat box and more like a disciplined console: lanes, gates, traces, voices, files, commits, and reconciled APIs. AI meets the ticket, but the ticket remains grounded in workflow.
F-SKU Sizing 101

Fabric F-SKUs are purchased capacity for a tenant or workspace estate. Each SKU gives a fixed number of Capacity Units (CU). Workspaces assigned to the capacity share that CU pool across Power BI, Data Factory, Data Engineering, Data Science, Real-Time Intelligence, Warehouse, and Lakehouse activity.

The simulator uses the same mental model an operator uses during an incident: compare concurrent CU demand against available SKU CU. Green means there is headroom, amber means monitor, orange means smoothing is absorbing pressure, and red means sustained demand exceeds the capacity envelope.

That is why the demo's thresholds are deliberately conservative. Under 50% utilization, there is room for mistakes. From 50% to 80%, teams should watch trends. From 80% to 100%, every new schedule or notebook matters. Above 100%, the operator should expect the capacity to spend down smoothing credits and eventually throttle.

The right response is not always an immediate scale-up. First, determine whether the pressure is interactive, background, or accidental. A user-facing DirectQuery peak deserves a different response than a forgotten notebook pool, an import refresh storm, or a dataflow that is scanning unchanged rows.
Capacity Units (CU): The Currency of Fabric

Capacity Units are the budget Fabric spends to execute work. A Spark session consumes CU based on driver and executor cores. A report query consumes CU while the visual renders. A pipeline consumes CU while activities orchestrate movement and transformation. The shared capacity is healthy when the total smoothed demand stays below the SKU's available CU.

For Spark notebooks, a practical rule from production operations is that one vCore is approximately one CU. An oversized environment with 8 driver cores and 8 executor cores can consume an entire F16. If dynamic allocation is disabled, that session can hold the capacity even while a user is between notebook cells.

The most useful dashboard question is not “what is the average usage?” It is “which workspace, item, or workload is holding CU during the peak?” The Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics app is the first stop for that answer because it breaks down utilization by item and operation.
Workload Profiles and Their CU Cost

The demo models six workload types. The CU values are intentionally simplified so the simulator is teachable: each selected workload contributes to per-user CU demand, and concurrency multiplies it. In real operations, the exact number depends on query shape, model design, Spark configuration, data size, cache state, and whether the work is interactive or background.
When Fabric Returns HTTP 430

HTTP 430 is the capacity signal. It is different from a generic API rate limit. In Fabric, a 430 means the capacity's smoothed usage has exceeded the allowed envelope and the service is protecting the capacity from more work. Operators often see this as failed notebook sessions, queued pipeline runs, delayed report renders, or API calls rejected during a peak.

Interactive throttling hurts users immediately because the person waiting for a visual, notebook cell, or SQL query is on the critical path. Background throttling is often less visible at first because scheduled jobs can be delayed, smoothed, or retried, but it still creates downstream freshness risk.
The Mitigation Playbook

A 430 is rarely solved by one change. The durable fix is a playbook: identify the consuming workload, reduce waste, move flexible work away from peaks, isolate blast radius, and then right-size the SKU with evidence.
1. Overnight scheduling

Use when: import refreshes, Dataflow Gen2 runs, Spark training, table maintenance, or pipeline batches are not user-facing. Move them into off-hours windows so background smoothing can spread load across the day instead of colliding with interactive BI hours.
2. Workspace splits

Use when: one domain or experimental team can starve everyone else. Assign high-risk workspaces to separate capacities, or at least separate production, non-production, and sandbox work. This turns a tenant-wide incident into a team-scoped one.
3. DirectLake migration

Use when: import refresh is burning CU just to copy data that already lives in OneLake. DirectLake can reduce refresh pressure by reading Delta files directly while preserving interactive report performance for suitable semantic models.
4. Pause non-prod outside business hours

Use when: dev, test, and sandbox capacities are idle overnight or on weekends. F-SKUs bill while running, so pause/resume automation can remove a large share of non-prod monthly spend without changing production posture.
5. Right-size workloads before right-sizing SKUs

Use when: Capacity Metrics shows a small number of items causing peaks. Fix oversized Spark environments, inefficient joins, unbounded queries, excessive refresh frequency, and polling loops before moving from F32 to F64.
PySpark Patterns That Save CU

PySpark is the place where small code choices can become large capacity events. The highest-return patterns are broadcast joins for small dimensions, predicate pushdown, partition pruning, compact file layouts, and Z-ordering columns used in filters and joins. These patterns reduce shuffle, scan fewer files, and shorten the time each session holds CU.

Notebook authors should also right-size Spark settings. Use dynamic allocation for interactive work, avoid fixed executor counts unless a job truly needs them, and reduce spark.sql.shuffle.partitions from the default when working on small or medium datasets.

from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast, col spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "8") spark.conf.set("spark.databricks.delta.optimizeWrite.enabled", "true") spark.conf.set("spark.databricks.delta.autoCompact.enabled", "true") orders = ( spark.table("lh_sales_slv.sales_orders_clean") .where((col("OrderDate") >= "2026-01-01") & (col("OrderDate") < "2026-02-01")) .select("OrderId", "CustomerId", "OrderDate", "NetAmount") ) customers = ( spark.table("lh_sales_slv.dim_customer") .select("CustomerId", "Segment", "Region") ) result = ( orders .join(broadcast(customers), "CustomerId", "left") .repartition("OrderDate") ) (result.write .format("delta") .mode("overwrite") .option("replaceWhere", "OrderDate >= '2026-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2026-02-01'") .saveAsTable("lh_sales_gld.fct_orders_month"))

The snippet keeps CU low by filtering early, selecting only needed columns, broadcasting a small dimension, partitioning the write by the date used for reruns, and avoiding a full-table overwrite. For large tables, pair this with Delta optimization and Z-ordering on high-selectivity columns used by report and warehouse queries.
Right-Sizing: F32 vs F64 vs Pause Strategy

Right-sizing starts with observed utilization, not fear. If an F32 is below 40% most of the week and only spikes during a nightly batch, the answer is probably scheduling or query tuning, not F64. If it spends business hours above 80% with interactive users waiting, F64 may be justified. If non-prod sits idle for 14 hours a day, pause strategy may save more than a downsize.

The practical operating loop is: observe seven days of Capacity Metrics, decompose by workspace and item, schedule flexible jobs away from the peak, mitigate inefficient patterns, and only then buy more CU. That loop keeps the platform reliable without turning every 430 into a procurement event.
1. The Medallion Architecture

The SPA shows a compact pipeline, but the pattern scales to a full data platform. Bronze, Silver, and Gold are separate Lakehouses so each layer has a clear contract. Bronze preserves the source record, Silver applies business rules and data quality gates, and Gold publishes curated facts, aggregates, and marts for analytics.

Fabric changes the center of gravity from database servers to OneLake. Instead of linked servers and stored procedures reaching across multiple machines, notebooks read committed Delta tables from the prior layer and write the next layer. The pipeline controls dependency order, but notebooks do not share memory; they communicate through persisted Delta tables.

2. Bronze: Raw Ingestion

Bronze is deliberately boring. It lands source data with minimal interpretation, adds audit columns, and keeps enough fidelity to replay or reprocess when downstream rules change. In a legacy migration, Bronze might start as JDBC extracts from a legacy SQL Server. In an event-driven design, Bronze receives file metadata or streaming events from Event Hub and Eventstream.

The important production lesson is that the ingestion trigger can evolve without rewriting the processing logic. A scheduled SFTP poll can become a storage event that flows through Event Hub, Fabric Eventstream, and Eventhouse. The downstream Data Pipeline still starts the same notebook chain; only the readiness signal changes from “the clock fired” to “the file or event arrived.”

# Bronze write pattern — raw landing with audit columns from pyspark.sql.functions import current_timestamp, lit source_table = "master_skip_trace" bronze_table = f"azsql_{source_table}_raw" df_bronze = ( df_source .withColumn("_brz_load_ts", current_timestamp()) .withColumn("_brz_source_table", lit(f"legacy_sql_server.dbo.{source_table}")) ) ( df_bronze.write .format("delta") .mode("append") .option("mergeSchema", "true") .saveAsTable(bronze_table) )

Schema-on-read is a strength at this layer. Bronze can absorb new source columns, retain raw payloads, and defer interpretation until Silver. That keeps ingestion resilient while preserving a complete audit trail for reconciliation.
3. Silver: Conformed & Cleansed

Silver is where the data platform earns trust. PySpark notebooks replace stored procedure logic with version-controlled code that can be tested locally, reviewed in Git, and promoted through environments. Typical Silver work includes casting strings to dates and decimals, deduplicating by business keys, applying joins that previously crossed SQL Server instances, hashing PII, and quarantining invalid records instead of silently publishing them.

Data quality gates belong here because Silver is the contract for downstream consumers. If a required key is missing, a status code is unknown, or a record violates a business invariant, the notebook should fail visibly or route the row to a quarantine table. Gold should never need to guess whether its inputs are trustworthy.

# Bronze to Silver — conformed, typed, and quality checked from pyspark.sql.functions import col, current_timestamp, sha2, concat_ws, lit, to_date bronze = spark.table("lh_loanetl_brz.dbo.azsql_master_skip_trace_raw") silver = ( bronze .filter(col("LoanID").isNotNull()) .dropDuplicates(["LoanID", "Record_Date"]) .withColumn("Record_Date", to_date(col("Record_Date"))) .withColumn("Phone_Hash", sha2(concat_ws("|", col("Phone"), lit("platform_salt")), 512)) .drop("Phone") .withColumn("_slv_processed_ts", current_timestamp()) ) invalid_count = silver.filter(col("Record_Date").isNull()).count() if invalid_count: raise ValueError(f"Data quality gate failed: {invalid_count} missing Record_Date values") ( silver.write .format("delta") .mode("overwrite") .option("replaceWhere", "Record_Date = '2026-05-09'") .saveAsTable("loanetl_batch_skip_trace_clean") )

4. Gold: Dimensional Models

Gold is intentionally smaller than Silver. It is shaped for analytics: facts at a clear grain, aggregates that avoid repeated expensive scans, and marts that align to business questions. The SPA's “Gold” and “Semantic Model” stages reflect this split: Spark publishes Delta tables, then Power BI semantic models define relationships, DAX measures, and presentation logic.

Direct Lake matters because Power BI can read Delta tables in OneLake without scheduled import copies. The result is a cleaner serving path: Gold tables stay in the Lakehouse, semantic definitions sit on top of them, and reports query governed data rather than disconnected extracts.

# Silver to Gold — dimensional facts and aggregates from pyspark.sql.functions import count, sum as spark_sum, current_timestamp silver = spark.table("lh_loanetl_slv.dbo.loanetl_batch_skip_trace_clean") fct_batch_skip_trace = ( silver .select("LoanID", "Record_Date", "Disposition", "Phone_Hash") .withColumn("_gld_published_ts", current_timestamp()) ) agg_daily_disposition = ( silver .groupBy("Record_Date", "Disposition") .agg( count("LoanID").alias("Loan_Count"), spark_sum("Attempt_Count").alias("Attempt_Count") ) .withColumn("_gld_published_ts", current_timestamp()) ) fct_batch_skip_trace.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("fct_batch_skip_trace") agg_daily_disposition.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("agg_skip_trace_daily")
5. Pipeline Orchestration

Fabric Data Pipelines replace the SQL Agent and SSIS pattern with an explicit dependency DAG. The pipeline can run notebooks sequentially, retry transient failures, pass parameters such as etl_process_date, and keep each activity observable. In the pilot pattern, Bronze must succeed before Silver starts, Silver must succeed before Gold starts, and maintenance can run after publication or on a separate schedule.

This is not the same mental model as a single stored procedure transaction. Fabric is choreographed, eventual, and asynchronous. Each notebook commits Delta tables; the next notebook reads those committed tables. That boundary makes reruns safer, troubleshooting clearer, and environment promotion easier.
6. OneLake Shortcuts

OneLake Shortcuts are the Fabric replacement for many linked-server and copy-heavy integration patterns. A table can physically live in one Lakehouse while another Lakehouse, Warehouse, or consuming workspace references it through a shortcut. The consumer sees a table-like object; the platform avoids duplicating the underlying Delta files.

This matters when Bronze data lands in Lakehouse A but multiple domains need to transform or enrich it in Lakehouse B. Instead of copying raw data into every workspace, the data platform can expose governed shortcuts. Teams get local-looking access while storage remains centralized and auditable.

# Conceptual read through a shortcut-backed table # Bronze physically lands in lh_source_brz. # lh_reporting_brz exposes it as a OneLake Shortcut, so the transform reads locally. raw_events = spark.table("lh_reporting_brz.dbo.azsql_transaction_events_raw") silver_events = ( raw_events .filter("event_type is not null") .dropDuplicates(["event_id"]) ) silver_events.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("platform_transaction_events_clean")

That is the key Build 2026 story: Fabric is not just a new place to run old database jobs. It is a governed data operating model where OneLake is the storage substrate, Spark handles transformation, Data Pipelines choreograph work, and Direct Lake semantic models serve analytics from the same Delta files.
0. The Sub-5-Minute Triage Loop

Every scenario below uses the same five-step shape, said out loud in an incident channel before diving into deep investigation. The target for the first five minutes is almost always mitigation — stopping user-facing impact — not a full root-cause fix. Separating those two explicitly is what keeps an incident bounded instead of turning into an open-ended debugging session.
1. Background: Forest Trusts and Transitivity

A forest is the top-level AD boundary — a set of domains sharing a schema, configuration partition, and global catalog. When two separate forests need to interoperate (common after mergers/acquisitions, or splitting a single company into separate security boundaries), you build a forest trust between the two forest root domains.
The property that comes up constantly in interviews is transitivity:

Practical framing for a "how would you link two AD forests" question: "I'd establish a two-way (or one-way, depending on trust direction needed) forest trust with selective authentication enabled, so users are trusted across the boundary but each resource domain still explicitly grants access rather than inheriting blanket authentication rights. That keeps the trust transitive at the namespace/routing level but access-controlled at the resource level."
2. Incident: "A GPO Isn't Applying to Some Machines in an OU"
Background: Two Ways to Scope a GPO
This is the one that trips people up because "scoping" sounds like one thing but AD gives you two independent scoping mechanisms that stack together.
A. Scoping by Linking (where the GPO applies structurally)

A GPO is a standalone object in the Group Policy Objects container — it does nothing until it's linked to a site, domain, or OU. Linking determines the structural scope: which part of the AD hierarchy the policy even has a chance to apply to. Link order and inheritance (with Block Inheritance / Enforced flags) control which GPO wins when multiple GPOs are linked up the tree.
B. Scoping by Security Filtering / WMI Filtering (who/what it applies to, within the linked scope)
Once a GPO is linked, you narrow who it actually applies to without moving objects between OUs:
Order of Precedence (the classic "LSDOU" + filtering)

Local policy → Site → Domain → OU (parent to child) ...then within the resolved link scope: Security filtering (ACL: Apply Group Policy = Allow) AND WMI filter match ...then conflict resolution: Enforced (No Override) GPOs win over Block Inheritance Last-applied (closest to the object, i.e. OU-level) wins on setting conflicts
3. Incident: "One Hostname Resolves to Two Different IPs"
Background: Why This Happens
A single FQDN resolving to two different IP addresses is not automatically a problem — it depends on why.
Legitimate reasons a hostname has multiple A/AAAA records
The problem case: stale/duplicate record from dynamic DNS registration

The more common troubleshooting scenario in an AD environment: a domain-joined computer or DC re-IPs (DHCP renewal, NIC change, re-image) and dynamic DNS registration (the client self-registering via ipconfig /registerdns or the Netlogon service) adds the new A record but the old one never aged out — because scavenging isn't enabled, or the record is static/manually created and won't be touched by scavenging at all.

Result: clients doing a lookup non-deterministically get routed to whichever record comes back first (or round-robin between both), so some connections succeed and some fail/timeout — intermittent, hard-to-reproduce connectivity complaints are the classic symptom.
Operational note: if it's a legitimate multi-homed host or load-balanced pair, leave both records but document it — the "fix" there is operational knowledge, not a DNS change.
4. Incident: Cross-Forest Auth Works, But a Downstream Call Fails ("Federated Transitive" Delegation)
Background: Why Auth Succeeds but Delegation Fails
This is almost certainly pointing at Kerberos constrained delegation across a forest trust, and the well-known failure mode when it's misconfigured.

6. General Incident-Management Loop (Beyond These Scenarios)
The same shape generalizes past AD/DNS/GPO to any on-call incident:
1. Azure Verified Modules (AVM) as the Building Blocks

The platform team standardizes Azure infrastructure on Bicep modules from the public module registry, especially Azure Verified Modules. AVM provides reviewed module contracts for common Azure resource types, so stack authors compose resource groups, identities, storage, networking, and platform services instead of hand-writing every ARM resource block.

This does not remove engineering judgment. Teams still decide naming, RBAC boundaries, tags, diagnostics, network posture, and lifecycle scope. AVM simply moves the low-level resource shape to a maintained baseline and lets the local stack focus on the platform pattern.

2. The Dual UMI Pattern (control-plane vs data-plane managed identities)

The SPA calls out two suffixes that matter: ctl and dat. A control-plane user-assigned managed identity deploys and updates infrastructure. A separate data-plane user-assigned managed identity is granted runtime access to Key Vault, Storage, Event Hubs, databases, and other workload services.

That separation prevents the deployment identity from becoming a universal runtime credential. It also makes reviews easier: control-plane RBAC answers “what can create or modify resources,” while data-plane RBAC answers “what can read or write workload data.”
3. OIDC Federated Identity (no long-lived secrets in GitHub Actions)

GitHub Actions authenticates to Azure with OpenID Connect federation. The job requests a short-lived token, Microsoft Entra ID validates the federated credential for the repository and environment, and azure/login receives an Azure access token. No client secret is stored in GitHub, copied into a runner, or rotated by hand.

The variables in this excerpt are non-secret identifiers: client ID, tenant ID, and subscription ID. Real tenant IDs and subscriptions are intentionally represented here with Microsoft Learn-style placeholders.

4. Deployment Stacks (vs traditional ARM deployments; deny-settings)

Traditional ARM or Bicep deployments apply a template to a scope, but lifecycle ownership can be ambiguous after the deployment finishes. Azure Deployment Stacks add a management layer around that deployment: Azure knows which resources belong to the stack, what should happen when resources disappear from the template, and whether unmanaged changes should be denied.

Deny settings are the sharp edge. They can block deletes or updates outside the stack, which makes production safer when used deliberately. The design goal is not to make emergencies impossible; it is to make out-of-band changes visible, time-bound, and followed by a PR so desired state catches up to reality.

az stack group create \ --name stk-skpapp-prd-usw2-001 \ --resource-group rg-skpapp-prd-usw2-001 \ --template-file stacks-bicep/skpapp/main.bicep \ --parameters stacks-bicep/skpapp/prd/main.prd.bicepparam \ --deny-settings-mode denyDelete \ --action-on-unmanage detachAll \ --yes
5. Trunk-Based CI/CD (main = production; feature branches via PR)

The delivery model is trunk-based. Engineers create short-lived feature branches, open pull requests, run validation, and merge through protected gates. The main branch represents production-ready desired state. If a bad change lands, the rollback path is a git revert rather than a hand-built undo script.

This is especially important for infrastructure. Portal edits, local az commands, and workspace clickops all create configuration drift. The governance pattern is simple: exploration can happen in dev, but production writes come from CI/CD using federated identity.
6. Modules, Stacks, and Composition (how main.bicep references AVM)

A stack folder contains the composition root: main.bicep, environment-specific main.{env}.bicepparam files, and optional dashboards or runbooks. The root Bicep file should read like a platform bill of materials. It wires AVM modules together, passes shared tags and naming variables, and exposes only the outputs that downstream workloads actually need.

The pattern keeps local modules rare. If a resource type exists in AVM, use the public registry reference first. If a custom wrapper is necessary, it should encode a platform standard that AVM does not cover, not repackage a single resource for convenience.

1. The JML Lifecycle

Joiner, mover, and leaver work is where identity administration becomes expensive. A new hire needs an account, baseline groups, a device, applications, and the right license bundle. A mover needs old permissions removed as deliberately as new permissions are added. A leaver needs access revoked quickly enough that security risk and license waste do not linger.

The demo models the lifecycle as an Entra-driven workflow rather than a ticket queue. HR or identity source changes trigger classification, group assignment, Intune enrollment, Conditional Access, and license reconciliation. The important point for Build 2026 is not that every step is fully automated on day one; it is that every manual gap has a visible cost.
2. Access Packages and Entitlement Management

Access packages move administration from individual group membership edits to requestable bundles. A package can represent a role such as Engineer, Manager, Finance reviewer, or Security operator. Each package has a catalog, eligibility rules, approval policy, expiration, and review cadence.

The SPA surfaces packages as role cards because that is how the business thinks about access. Users do not ask for ten group names; they ask for the tools needed to do a job. Entitlement management translates that job request into time-bound memberships that can be approved, reviewed, and removed.
Package Design Pattern

Role package → business-readable bundle of groups and apps Eligibility → who may request it Approval → role owner or manager validates the need Expiration → access ends unless actively renewed Review cadence → stale access is found before audit season
3. PIM-Gated Admin Roles

Administrative access should be eligible by default and active only when there is a reason. Privileged Identity Management separates the right to request a role from the act of holding that role. That distinction is central for Global Admin, Privileged Role Admin, Security Admin, Exchange Admin, Intune Admin, and Helpdesk roles.

The runbook pattern behind the article is simple: grant eligible membership to a protected group, require justification, cap activation duration, and let the activation expire. Emergency procedures can still exist, but they should create a short-lived audit trail instead of permanent standing access.
4. Intune as the Endpoint Backbone

Identity controls are only as strong as the endpoint posture behind them. Intune gives the tenant an operating surface for Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android devices: enrollment, Autopilot, compliance policy, configuration profile, application deployment, and remote actions.

The SPA includes compliance bars because endpoint state should be visible next to access state. Conditional Access can require compliant devices before users reach M365 resources, Copilot experiences, or sensitive applications. That means a Joiner flow is not complete when the account exists; it is complete when the device is enrolled, compliant, and governed.
5. M365 Copilot Licensing and Governance

M365 Copilot is a per-user add-on layered on top of the tenant's data, identity, and compliance posture. The license unlocks the experience, but governance determines whether the experience is safe and useful. Sensitivity labels, DLP policy, SharePoint permissions, audit logging, pilot scope, and cost approval should be in place before broad enablement.

The core governance question is not only “who gets Copilot?” It is “what can Copilot retrieve for that user?” Copilot respects existing permissions, so over-broad SharePoint or Teams access becomes over-broad AI retrieval. Readiness work therefore starts with permissions hygiene and a small pilot group before expanding.
6. Copilot Agents and the Vendor Risk Picture

Copilot agents make the governance story more complicated because each agent introduces a source, an action surface, and a data handling model. First-party Teams meeting recap is different from a third-party connector, and a read-only retrieval agent is different from an agent that writes back to a system.

The SPA references agents such as Confluence search, project planning, and Teams meeting summaries because they are realistic productivity wins. The risk review should still ask the same questions every time: what data source is queried, whose identity is used, whether writes are possible, how citations work, and whether logs can prove what happened.
Agent Vetting Checklist

1. Identify the data source and whether it stays inside the tenant. 2. Confirm the agent uses delegated user access, not broad service-account access. 3. Require citations so humans can verify source material. 4. Block sensitive data classes that do not belong in prompts. 5. Log user, timestamp, prompt class, response class, and source links. 6. Review residual risk before expanding beyond the pilot group.
1. The Three-Tier Workspace Model

The console models Fabric onboarding as a tiered service instead of a one-off administrator task. Sandbox, Dev, and Prod have different permissions, gates, and expectations. That split matters because the right answer for experimentation is not the right answer for production reporting.

Sandbox workspaces give engineers a safe place to learn, run notebooks, and use synthetic data. Dev workspaces integrate team work behind a repository. Prod workspaces are deployment targets that serve downstream consumers and should not be edited manually.
2. Self-Service Onboarding

Self-service starts with a structured request. A team describes the workload, expected source systems, row volume, refresh schedule, users, and downstream consumers. The platform team turns that request into a standard workspace plan rather than inventing a new topology each time.

The handoff is automated where possible and explicit where human judgment is needed. Intake captures enough detail to choose the domain name, environment set, Git repository, parameter files, security groups, and whether a sandbox is needed before the team touches production-bound assets.
Onboarding Contract

request: workload: "<domain-or-product-name>" team: "<application-team-or-data-team>" sources: ["<source-system>"] refresh: "<hourly|daily|weekly>" environments: ["sandbox", "dev", "prod"] downstream_consumers: ["<report-or-api-consumer>"] documentation_owner: "<role-label>"
3. PIM-Gated Production Access

Production access is not a permanent entitlement in the model shown by the SPA. Users can be eligible for elevated roles while remaining inactive by default. When a deployment, incident, or operational task requires write access, the role is activated with a duration and justification.

This keeps least privilege operationally realistic. Reader assignments support normal observation. Contributor or administrator paths are time-bound and auditable. The console's PIM tab represents that distinction by showing role, scope, duration, and justification together.
4. Backlog Management

The provisioning console fits into a flow-based backlog model. Requests enter a queue, are pulled into active work when capacity exists, move to waiting when blocked by approvals or external dependencies, and finish as done only when the workspace and documentation are usable.

This model prevents platform intake from becoming an invisible pile of favors. Each request has a state, a constraint, and a next action. Waiting work does not consume the active work-in-progress slot, but it stays visible so follow-up does not rely on memory.
Queue Discipline

Identified → Named & Scored → Queued → Active → Waiting or Done Rule of thumb: - Pull only when capacity exists. - Keep one active item per lane. - Move blocked work to waiting with an explicit next action. - Finish by documenting how the team operates the workspace.

1. Why Event-Driven

Polling works until the first real incident. A pull-based job asks every source, on a schedule, whether anything interesting happened. That creates idle reads during quiet periods and delayed visibility during spikes. The better pattern is to make every producer publish a durable event as soon as the fact exists.

In this design, services emit JSON to an Azure Event Hub namespace such as evhns-secops-prd-.... Event Hub provides the shock absorber: partitioned throughput, consumer groups, retention, replay, and a simple contract that producers can target without knowing where analytics data lands.

The SPA mirrors that model. Its ClojureScript demo renders a live stream, stage cards, and a KQL panel for the path from Clojure Functions to Event Hub, Eventstream, Eventhouse, parsed KQL tables, and Gold Lakehouse outputs.
2. The Kappa Architecture

Kappa architecture uses one pipeline for both stream and batch-style outcomes. Instead of copying the same log through Bronze, Silver, and Gold Lakehouses with notebooks at each hop, raw events land once in Eventhouse and KQL derives the shaped views, functions, update policies, and materialized views above it.

That makes the operational boundary cleaner. Platform engineering owns the plumbing: Event Hub, Eventstream, Eventhouse, identity, and retention. Application and security teams own their KQL: parsing rules, alert logic, dashboard views, and department-specific aggregations.

The practical advantage is accountability. If a service adds a field, the producer contract and KQL parser change together. There is no chained notebook dependency that has to be rescheduled before the dashboard becomes useful again.
Common Alert Query

let window = 5m; transaction_parsed | where ingestion_time() > ago(window) | where severity in ('P1', 'Critical') or status_code >= 500 | summarize event_count = count(), impacted_services = dcount(service_name), sample_trace = any(trace_id), latest_event = max(timestamp) by alert_key = strcat(service_name, ':', tostring(status_code)), service_name | where event_count >= 3 | project latest_event, alert_key, service_name, event_count, impacted_services, sample_trace

This style of query is intentionally small and operational. It groups related failures, preserves a trace sample for investigation, and produces a stable alert_key that the orchestration layer can use for deduplication.
3. Eventstream as the Glue

Fabric Eventstream is the managed connector layer between Event Hub and Eventhouse. It removes the need to operate a Kafka cluster, patch brokers, rebalance partitions, or maintain a custom event processor just to move records into the analytical store.

The important capacity pattern is to avoid one Eventstream per source. A workspace should use one Eventstream where practical, with multiple sources in and multiple destinations out. Routing can use event properties such as source, eventType, or route to send records to the correct KQL table.

For the security platform, this means activity logs, application health checks, alert actions, and policy compliance events can share the same managed event-processing backbone while still landing in separate raw tables for clean ownership and replay.
4. Eventhouse + KQL

Eventhouse is the hot analytical tier. Raw tables capture the event exactly as received; parsed tables make those events queryable; materialized views pre-aggregate common operational questions such as failures by service, latency bands, and active security alerts.

KQL is the right language for this workload because it is built for time windows, pattern matching, dynamic JSON, summarization, and interactive investigation. Operators can move from an alert tile to a trace-level query without switching storage engines.

The SPA's KQL update-policy panel is a simplified version of this contract. A raw event is parsed into typed columns: timestamp, service name, level, status code, and message. Production queries extend that with correlation IDs, resource IDs, tenant placeholders, normalized severity, and alert routing keys.

5. Retention Tiers

Retention is a cost and usability decision. The hot tier should keep enough data for incident response, failed deployment triage, and short-term trend analysis. Older data should remain discoverable, but it does not need the same compute profile as an active outage.

This tiering strategy avoids treating every byte as a premium SIEM record forever. Security-relevant detections can still flow to Microsoft Sentinel or downstream incident systems, while high-volume telemetry uses the storage and query engine that matches its lifecycle.
6. Alert Orchestration

Alerting is where real-time analytics becomes operations. A KQL query can identify candidate alerts, but a durable workflow decides what to do next: deduplicate repeated signals, suppress known maintenance windows, create tickets, send Teams cards, email on-call roles, and mark the alert as ticketed.

Azure Durable Functions fits this pattern because the fan-out/fan-in model is explicit. One orchestrator reads the active alert set, starts one activity per alert, waits for completion, records outcomes, and can retry transient failures without sending duplicate notifications.

The security platform uses this separation to keep detection logic in KQL and side effects in code. KQL answers, “What is happening?” Durable Functions answers, “Who needs to know, and have we already told them?”
Operational Guardrails

A production version of this pipeline needs guardrails that are visible to both platform and application teams. Each producer should publish a versioned envelope, include a trace identifier, and avoid placing secrets or personal data in message bodies.

Each ingestion component should also expose health signals. Event Hub lag, Eventstream destination failures, Eventhouse ingestion errors, and Durable Function retry counts are separate failure modes. Treating them separately makes incident triage faster.

The runbook should include a replay path. Event Hub retention and Eventhouse ingestion tracking make it possible to replay a small window after a parser fix without asking application teams to re-emit historical events.

The pattern is intentionally Microsoft-native. Event Hubs absorbs producer traffic, Fabric Real-Time Intelligence handles streaming and KQL analytics, OneLake provides the lake boundary, Durable Functions coordinates side effects, and Sentinel remains available for security correlation where SIEM semantics are required.

That mix matters because the goal is not to build another bespoke logging platform. The goal is to make operational telemetry queryable within seconds, keep long-term storage economical, and preserve a clear path from detection to accountable action.

The end result is a pipeline that is real-time without being fragile: event-driven ingestion, managed stream routing, hot KQL analytics, lifecycle-aware retention, and durable alert handling that can be explained from the SPA all the way to production architecture.

1. The File-Driven Mental Model

Workflow Toolkit starts with a small refusal: the operational source of truth does not have to live inside a browser tab. Browser SaaS tools remain the official systems of record, but the working state lives in a repository. A Jira issue is represented by an issue file. A ServiceDesk Plus request is represented by a case file. A daily plan is represented by a planner note. The operator edits those files with the same tools used for code.

That shift matters for AI operations. An agent can reason over a markdown file without screen scraping, hidden modal state, or a brittle browser session. It can propose a worklog, add a follow-up, update a flow label, or prepare a standup summary in a form that a human can review before anything touches an external API.

The pattern is deliberately boring: capture the work, encode it as text, commit it, and let automation reconcile it. The boring part is the feature. Text has history. Git has review. CI has repeatability. Markdown has enough structure to be parsed by scripts and enough flexibility to be useful during messy investigations.

The repository boundary also gives the operator a clean trust boundary. AI can draft file changes. Git shows the diff. GitHub Actions turns accepted changes into API calls. If a run fails, the markdown remains intact and the next run can pick up from the same durable state.
